<p><strong>How to Make Sushi Rice</strong> is the foundation of great sushi. Perfectly cooked Japanese rice, seasoned while hot with a simple vinegar mixture, gives you glossy grains with a balanced sweet and tangy flavor. I’ll share the exact method I use so your sushi rice turns out right every time.</p>



<ul class="wp-block-list is-style-heart">
<li>Consistently <strong>shiny, plump, well-seasoned</strong> rice</li>



<li>Uses the <strong>golden rice-to-water ratio</strong> for the perfect texture</li>



<li>Easy <strong>homemade sushi vinegar</strong> with 3 pantry ingredients</li>
</ul>

<h2 class="wp-block-heading" id="h-what-is-sushi-rice">What is Sushi Rice?</h2>



<p><strong>Sushi rice</strong> dates back to ancient <em>narezushi</em>, where rice was used to ferment and preserve fish. Over time, vinegar replaced fermentation to create the same lightly sour taste. Sushi evolved again in the 1600s to use vinegared rice and fresh fish in<strong> <em>hayazushi</em> </strong>or “fast sushi.” Known as <em>shari</em> (シャリ), <em>sushi-meshi</em> (鮨飯), or <em>su-meshi</em> (酢飯), seasoned rice today is the foundation of modern sushi.</p>

		</div>		
		


<h2 class="wp-block-heading" id="h-ingredients-for-sushi-rice">Ingredients for Sushi Rice</h2>



<ul class="wp-block-list">
<li>Japanese short-grain white rice</li>



<li>kombu (dried kelp) – optional</li>



<li>Japanese rice vinegar (unseasoned)</li>



<li>sugar</li>



<li>salt</li>
</ul>



<p><em>Find the <strong>printable recipe</strong> with measurements below. </em></p>

<h2 class="wp-block-heading" id="h-how-to-make-sushi-rice"><strong>How to Make Sushi Rice</strong></h2>



<ol class="wp-block-list">
<li><span style="box-sizing: border-box; margin: 0px; padding: 0px;"><strong>Wash and cook the rice. </strong>Rinse the rice several times until the water runs clear. Drain well, then add it to the rice cooker with the measured cold water and kombu. Let the rinsed rice soak for 20–30 minutes.</span> Cook using the Sushi setting, if available. </li>
</ol>



<ol start="2" class="wp-block-list">
<li><strong>Make the rice seasoning.</strong> Meanwhile, gently heat the rice vinegar, sugar, and salt in a small saucepan on the stove over medium-high heat to a near boil. Cool.</li>
</ol>



<ol start="3" class="wp-block-list">
<li><strong>Season the cooked rice.</strong> Remove the kombu and transfer the hot rice to a wooden <a href="https://amzn.to/3WLIsMj" target="_blank" rel="noopener nofollow" data-wpel-link="external" class="ext-link">sushi <em>oke</em></a><em> </em>(called <em>hangiri),</em> baking sheet, or wide large bowl. Spread it out so steam can escape. Pour the cooled sushi vinegar over the hot rice, using a rice paddle to control the flow.</li>
</ol>



<ol start="4" class="wp-block-list">
<li><strong>“Slice” the rice and let cool.</strong> Hold the rice paddle at a 45-degree angle and use a slicing motion to distribute the seasoned vinegar and break up clumps while fanning the rice. Flip gently until glossy and cooled.</li>
</ol>



<ol start="5" class="wp-block-list">
<li><strong>Serve.</strong> Cover with a damp towel or paper towel and use it at room temperature.</li>
</ol>

<h2 class="wp-block-heading" id="h-nami-s-recipe-tips">Nami’s Recipe Tips</h2>



<p>These simple tips will help you make <strong>sushi rice</strong> successfully every time.</p>



<ul class="wp-block-list is-style-check">
<li><strong>To save time, use bottled <a href="https://amzn.to/4aabVpf" target="_blank" rel="noopener nofollow" data-wpel-link="external" class="ext-link">sushi vinegar (seasoned rice vinegar)</a></strong>, also called  <em>sushizu</em> (すし酢), instead of making it from scratch.</li>
</ul>



<ul class="wp-block-list is-style-check">
<li><strong>If you make it at home, use <a href="https://amzn.to/4qAAl0Z" target="_blank" rel="noopener nofollow" data-wpel-link="external" class="ext-link">Japanese rice vinegar</a></strong>—It has a mild flavor for an authentic taste.</li>
</ul>



<ul class="wp-block-list is-style-check">
<li><strong>Use less water (1:1 rice-to-water ratio).</strong> This keeps the rice from turning mushy after adding seasoned rice vinegar.</li>
</ul>



<ul class="wp-block-list is-style-check">
<li><strong>Cook rice with kombu, if you like.</strong> A small piece adds gentle aroma and umami, though it’s optional.</li>
</ul>



<ul class="wp-block-list is-style-check">
<li><strong>Season the rice while hot.</strong> Hot rice absorbs the vinegar evenly.</li>
</ul>



<ul class="wp-block-list is-style-check">
<li><strong>Use a slicing motion and cool quickly.</strong> Stirring breaks the grains and makes the rice mushy. Gently fan to remove excess moisture and add shine.</li>
</ul>



<ul class="wp-block-list is-style-check">
<li><strong>Don’t forget to cover with a damp towel.</strong> This keeps the rice from drying out while you make sushi.</li>
</ul>



<ul class="wp-block-list is-style-check">
<li><strong>Use a <em><a href="https://amzn.to/3WLIsMj" target="_blank" rel="noopener nofollow" data-wpel-link="external" class="ext-link">hangiri (sushi oke)</a></em> or a large tray</strong>, such as a baking sheet. A hangiri is the traditional vessel for seasoning the rice. It makes it easy to spread out hot rice and cool it after adding the sushi vinegar, and the <em>hinoki</em> (cypress) wood absorbs excess moisture. Lightly moisten it with water before adding the rice. </li>
</ul>

<h2 class="wp-block-heading" id="h-storage-tips">Storage Tips</h2>



<p class="is-style-arrow"><strong>To store:</strong> Transfer leftover rice to an airtight container and freeze. Do not refrigerate.</p>



<p class="is-style-arrow"><strong>To reheat:</strong> Bring frozen rice back to room temperature before using. Do not microwave.</p>



<h2 class="wp-block-heading" id="h-faqs">FAQs</h2>


		<div class="mainsection togglelist notop nobot">
			

			<div class="toggleitem" id="faqitem-what-is-the-best-rice-for-sushi">
				<h3 tabindex="0" role="button" class="wp-block-heading" id="h-what-is-the-best-rice-for-sushi">What is the best rice for sushi?</h3>				<div class="togglereveal notop nobot">
					



<p>Japanese <strong>short-grain</strong> white rice has the ideal balance of moisture and firmness and that’s what I use. In the U.S., California grown medium-grain white rice is commonly used for sushi rice. Long-grain, jasmine, or brown rice will not hold together properly.</p>



<p>For short-grain substitute, I recommend Korean short-grain white rice, which is quite similar to Japanese short-grain white rice.</p>
				</div>
			</div>
					</div>
		

		<div class="mainsection togglelist notop nobot">
			

			<div class="toggleitem" id="faqitem-what-is-sushi-rice-seasoning-made-of">
				<h3 tabindex="0" role="button" class="wp-block-heading" id="h-what-is-sushi-rice-seasoning-made-of">What is sushi rice seasoning made of?</h3>				<div class="togglereveal notop nobot">
					



<p>Sushi rice seasoning is made from unseasoned Japanese rice vinegar, sugar, and salt, creating the signature sweet, salty, and tangy flavor.</p>
				</div>
			</div>
					</div>
		

		<div class="mainsection togglelist notop nobot">
			

			<div class="toggleitem" id="faqitem-why-is-my-sushi-rice-mushy">
				<h3 tabindex="0" role="button" class="wp-block-heading" id="h-why-is-my-sushi-rice-mushy">Why is my sushi rice mushy?</h3>				<div class="togglereveal notop nobot">
					



<p>Sushi rice turns mushy when it’s cooked with too much water. Use equal parts rice and water—slightly less than regular steamed rice since you’ll add sushi vinegar later. Make sure to season the rice while it’s hot. Also, sushi rice gets mushy when it’s stirred too much so make sure to gently slice and fold instead of stirring.</p>
				</div>
			</div>
					</div>

	<div id="recipe-60671-notes" class="wprm-recipe-notes-container wprm-block-text-normal"><h3 id="toc-notes" class="wprm-recipe-header wprm-recipe-notes-header wprm-block-text-bold wprm-align-left wprm-header-decoration-none" style="">Notes</h3><div class="wprm-recipe-notes"><h5 id="toc-whats-the-measurement-for-1-rice-cooker-cup" class="p1"><strong>What’s the measurement for 1 rice cooker cup?</strong></h5>
<ul>
<li>The plastic <b>rice cooker cup</b> that comes with the rice cooker is <b>¾ cup (180 ml)</b>. In Japan, this amount is called <b>ichi go</b> (<span class="s1">一合</span>).</li>
<li>One rice cooker cup of uncooked short-grain Japanese rice is <strong>150 grams</strong>.</li>
</ul>
<h5 id="toc-how-much-rice-do-you-need-to-make"><strong>How much rice do you need to make?</strong></h5>
<ul class="ul1">
<li class="li1"><b>1 </b><b><i>rice cooker</i></b><b> cup</b> (180 ml, ¾ cup, 150 g) of uncooked rice makes <strong>2¼ cups</strong> (330 g) of cooked rice.
<ul class="ul1">
<li class="li1">1 <b>thick</b> sushi roll</li>
<li class="li1">2 <b>medium</b> sushi rolls</li>
<li class="li1">4 <b>thin</b> sushi rolls</li>
<li class="li1">3 <b>inside-out</b> rolls</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li class="li1"><b>2 </b><b><i>rice cooker</i></b><b> cups</b> (360 ml, 1½ cups, 300 g) of uncooked rice make <strong>4⅓ cups </strong>(660 g) of cooked rice.
<ul class="ul1">
<li class="li1">2 <b>thick</b> sushi rolls</li>
<li class="li1">4 <b>medium</b> sushi rolls</li>
<li class="li1">8 <b>thin</b> sushi rolls</li>
<li class="li1">6 <b>inside-out</b> sushi rolls</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li class="li1"><b>3 </b><b><i>rice cooker</i></b><b> cups</b> (540 ml, 2¼ cups, 450 g) of uncooked rice make <strong>6⅔ cups</strong> (990 g) of cooked rice.
<ul class="ul1">
<li class="li1">4 <b>thick</b> sushi rolls</li>
<li class="li1">6 <b>medium</b> sushi rolls</li>
<li class="li1">12 <b>thin</b> sushi rolls</li>
<li class="li1">9 <b>inside-out</b> sushi rolls</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li class="li1"><b>4 </b><b><i>rice cooker</i></b><b> cups</b> (720 ml, 3 cups, 600 g) of uncooked rice make <strong>8¾ cups</strong> (1320 g) of cooked rice.
<ul class="ul1">
<li class="li1">5 <b>thick</b> sushi rolls</li>
<li class="li1">8 <b>medium</b> sushi rolls</li>
<li class="li1">16 <b>thin</b> sushi rolls</li>
<li class="li1">12 <b>inside-out</b> sushi rolls</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li class="li1"><b>5 </b><b><i>rice cooker</i></b><b> cups</b> (900 ml, 3¾ cups, 750 g) of uncooked rice make <strong>11 cups</strong> (1650 g) of cooked rice.
<ul class="ul1">
<li class="li1">6 <b>thick</b> sushi rolls</li>
<li class="li1">11 <b>medium</b> sushi rolls</li>
<li class="li1">20 <b>thin</b> sushi rolls</li>
<li class="li1">15 <b>inside-out</b> sushi rolls</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
<h5 id="toc-how-much-prepared-sushi-rice-do-you-need-for-one-sushi-roll" class="p1"><strong>How much prepared sushi rice do you need for one sushi roll?</strong></h5>
<ul class="ul1">
<li class="li1">One <b>thick</b> sushi roll (<a href="https://www.justonecookbook.com/futomaki/" data-wpel-link="internal"><span class="s2"><i>Futomaki</i></span></a>) requires 1⅔ cups (250 g) of prepared sushi rice.</li>
<li class="li1">One <b>medium</b> sushi roll (<i>Chumaki</i>), like <a href="https://www.justonecookbook.com/vegetarian-sushi-rolls/" data-wpel-link="internal"><span class="s2">Vegetarian Sushi Roll</span></a>, requires 1 cup (150 g) of sushi rice.</li>
<li class="li1">One <b>thin</b> sushi roll (<a href="https://www.justonecookbook.com/sushi-rolls/" data-wpel-link="internal"><span class="s2"><i>Hosomaki</i></span></a>) requires ½ cup (80 g) of sushi rice.</li>
<li class="li1">One <b>inside-out</b> sushi roll (<i>Uramaki</i>), like <a href="https://www.justonecookbook.com/california-roll/" data-wpel-link="internal"><span class="s2">California Roll</span></a>, requires ¾ cup (110 g) of sushi rice.</li>
<li class="li1">One <b><i>nigiri</i></b> sushi requires 20 g of sushi rice.</li>
</ul></div></div>
